title: Das Todtenhemdchen
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 109. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß).
about: KHM 109 runs to a single short paragraph, and is among the most quietly devastating tales in the collection: a mother weeps without ceasing for her dead seven-year-old, who appears to her each night, until the child finally speaks — its little shroud, it says, cannot dry from her tears, and it begs her to stop so it can rest. No moral is appended; the grief and the child's request are left to stand on their own.

sentences.t: Es hatte eine Mutter ein Büblein von sieben Jahren, das war so schön und lieblich, daß es niemand ansehen konnte ohne ihm gut zu sein, und sie hatte es auch lieber als alles auf der Welt.
sentences.l: A mother had a little-boy of seven years, that was so fair and lovely that no one could look at it without being kind to it, and she had it dearer, too, than everything in the world.
sentences.i: A mother had a little boy of seven, who was so fair and lovely that no one could look at him without growing fond of him, and she loved him more than anything in the world.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with the dummy subject “es” holding the front slot (“Es hatte eine Mutter …”), which English drops. “Büblein” is a diminutive and so neuter, and the German goes on calling the child “es” — “it” — all through the tale; the idiomatic line says “he.” “lieb haben,” in the comparative “lieber haben als,” is the ordinary way of saying one loves something more.

sentences.t: Nun geschah es, daß es plötzlich krank ward, und der liebe Gott es zu sich nahm;
sentences.l: Now it happened that it suddenly became sick, and the dear God took it to himself;
sentences.i: Now it came to pass that he suddenly fell ill, and the dear God took him to himself;
sentences.n: “ward” is the older preterite of werden (modern wurde) — you will meet it constantly in these tales. “zu sich nehmen,” to take to oneself, is the gentle way German says that God has taken someone in death.

sentences.t: darüber konnte sich die Mutter nicht trösten und weinte Tag und Nacht.
sentences.l: over that the mother could not console herself and wept day and night.
sentences.i: the mother could not be comforted for it, and wept day and night.
sentences.n: “darüber” (da- + über) points back at what has just been said: ‘over that.’ “sich trösten” is reflexive — to console oneself, to be comforted.

sentences.t: Bald darauf aber, nachdem es begraben war, zeigte sich das Kind Nachts an den Plätzen, wo es sonst im Leben gesessen und gespielt hatte;
sentences.l: Soon after that, however, after it had been buried, the child showed itself at night in the places where it had otherwise sat and played in life;
sentences.i: Soon after, however, once he had been buried, the child appeared at night in the places where he used to sit and play when alive;
sentences.n: “Nachts” is an adverbial genitive, ‘by night.’ “sonst” here means ‘at other times, formerly,’ not ‘otherwise.’ German prefers “sich zeigen” — to show itself — where English says something appeared.

sentences.t: weinte die Mutter, so weinte es auch, und wenn der Morgen kam, war es verschwunden.
sentences.l: wept the mother, so wept it too, and when the morning came, it was vanished.
sentences.i: if the mother wept, the child wept too; and when morning came, he was gone.
sentences.n: A conditional with no wenn: putting the verb first (“weinte die Mutter, so …”) means ‘if the mother wept, then …’, and the answering “so” in the second half is what marks it.

sentences.t: Als aber die Mutter gar nicht aufhören wollte zu weinen, kam es in einer Nacht mit seinem weißen Todtenhemdchen, in welchem es in den Sarg gelegt war, und mit dem Kränzchen auf dem Kopf,
sentences.l: But when the mother would not leave off weeping at all, it came one night with its white little-shroud, in which it had been laid in the coffin, and with the little wreath on its head,
sentences.i: But when the mother would not stop weeping at all, he came one night in his white little shroud, the one he had been laid in the coffin in, and with the little wreath on his head,
sentences.n: “Todtenhemdchen” is the 1857 spelling of Totenhemdchen, the little shift a dead child was dressed in for burial; the “Kränzchen,” a small wreath, went on the head with it. “gar nicht” strengthens the negative: not at all.

sentences.t: setzte sich zu ihren Füßen auf das Bett und sprach „ach Mutter, höre doch auf zu weinen, sonst kann ich in meinem Sarge nicht einschlafen, denn mein Todtenhemdchen wird nicht trocken von deinen Thränen, die alle darauf fallen.“
sentences.l: [it] set itself down at her feet on the bed and said, “ah mother, do leave off weeping, otherwise I cannot fall asleep in my coffin, for my little-shroud will not go dry from your tears, which all fall on it.”
sentences.i: he sat down at her feet on the bed and said, “oh mother, do stop crying, or I cannot fall asleep in my coffin, for my little shroud will not dry, with all your tears falling on it.”
sentences.n: The subject is still the child from the sentence before, so the German simply carries on with the next verb; the “[it]” in the literal line is supplied here in square brackets, which mark words added here and never words in the 1857 text. “höre … auf” is separable aufhören, ‘to leave off,’ with the particle at the end of its clause. “Sarge” keeps the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Da erschrack die Mutter, als sie das hörte, und weinte nicht mehr.
sentences.l: Then the mother took fright, when she heard that, and wept no more.
sentences.i: At that the mother took fright, hearing it, and wept no more.
sentences.n: “erschrack” is the 1857 spelling of erschrak, preterite of erschrecken in its intransitive sense — to be startled, to take fright — as against the transitive ‘to frighten someone.’

sentences.t: Und in der andern Nacht kam das Kindchen wieder, hielt in der Hand ein Lichtchen und sagte „siehst du, nun ist mein Hemdchen bald trocken, und ich habe Ruhe in meinem Grab.“
sentences.l: And in the other night the little-child came again, held in the hand a little light and said, “you see, now my little-shirt is soon dry, and I have rest in my grave.”
sentences.i: And the next night the little child came again, holding a little light in his hand, and said, “you see, now my little shift is nearly dry, and I have rest in my grave.”
sentences.n: “in der andern Nacht” — “ander” here means ‘the next,’ not ‘the other.’ “bald trocken” is ‘soon dry,’ i.e. nearly dry. The diminutives pile up in this tale — Büblein, Todtenhemdchen, Kränzchen, Kindchen, Lichtchen, Bettchen — and every one of them is neuter.

sentences.t: Da befahl die Mutter dem lieben Gott ihr Leid und ertrug es still und geduldig, und das Kind kam nicht wieder, sondern schlief in seinem unterirdischen Bettchen.
sentences.l: Then the mother commended her sorrow to the dear God and bore it quietly and patiently, and the child came not again, but slept in its underground little-bed.
sentences.i: Then the mother gave her sorrow over into the keeping of the dear God and bore it quietly and patiently, and the child did not come again, but slept on in its little bed under the earth.
sentences.n: “befehlen” here is not ‘to command’ but the older sense ‘to commit, commend into someone’s keeping’ — the mother hands her grief to God. The tale closes with one more diminutive: the “Bettchen,” the little bed, is the grave.

glossary.ansehen: ansehen — to look at (infinitive; es ansehen konnte: could look at it); also das Ansehen, the looking, regard
glossary.befahl: befehlen — commended, committed (3rd sg. preterite; jemandem etwas befehlen: to give something into someone’s keeping; more usually ‘commanded, ordered’)
glossary.es: es — it (the little boy: Büblein is a diminutive and so neuter, and the tale calls the child “es” throughout); also the dummy subject that opens a tale, Es hatte eine Mutter …
glossary.höre: aufhören — leave off, stop (2nd sg. imperative, separable: höre … auf); also höre, ‘I hear,’ from hören
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, to it (dative; here of the boy, whom the German keeps calling by the neuter “es”)
glossary.lieber: lieb — dearer (comparative, in lieber haben als: to love more than anything); also lieber, the inflected adjective ‘dear’ (lieber Gott)
